Rokya Begum  ------ Petitioner.
Vs.

full_judgment:
This Rule arises out of a proceeding for preemption which was originally started under section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

 2. The property in question belonged to two brothers, namely, Gopal Chandra Das and Radha Gobinda Das, of whom Gopal Chandra Das was insane. Radha Gobinda Das having sold the disputed land by a kabala dated 14.11.60 for a sum of Tk. 400/- to the petitioner, an application under section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was filed on the 22nd July, 1965 by Gopal Chandra Das through one Suren Chandra as his next friend on the allegation that Gopal Chandra was insane and the applicant's date of the knowledge about the sale under pre-emption was the 23rd April, 1965. On the 28th March, 1966 the said Suren Chandra Das was removed as the next friend of the applicant, who was thereafter represented by one Promatha Nath Sarker as his next friend. At the time of the hearing Suren Chandra Das was examined as a witness on behalf of the opposite party in the said case. The pre-emption proceeding was ultimately dismissed by the trial Court on the grounds that the formalities enjoined under section 96 of the Act as to the statement about the total quantity of the land in possession of the applicant was not complied with and also that the story that the purchaser having not been in possession of the purchased land, the applicant was not at all aware of the sale under pre-emption, was not believable and as such the proceeding was barred by limitation. The purchaser's further case that she made an improvement of the land costing about Tk. 1200/ was also not accepted. The application having failed, an appeal against the said order of dismissal was filed, and the appeal was allowed by the Subordinate Judge, Rajshahi on the finding that the applicant had no knowledge of the sale earlier than the date alleged in the application and as such the application was not barred by limitation. The learned Sub ordinate Judge further held that it being stated in the application that the applicant had not more than 20 bighas of land and this statement having not been denied in the written objection, it cannot be said that the requirement of section 96 as to the ceiling of the land in possession was not complied with. 

 4. Mr. Akram Hossain Amin, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner submits that although the application has been purported to have been filed under Section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, this application should be treated as an application under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act in as much as the right of pre-emption has accrued at the time when the provisions of Bengal Tenancy Act were in force in the area in which the lands under pre-emption are situated. The learned Advocate has contended that the period of limitation under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act in case of a non-notified co-sharer is 3 years from the date of the sale, and that the present application having been filed long after three years from the date of the sale, the Court of appeal acted illegally in the exercise of its jurisdiction in allowing the said application. 

 5. It has been stated in the application that Part V of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 which includes section 96 of the Act came into operation on the 1st August, 1963 in the District of Rajshahi wherein the land under. Pre-emption lies. The right of pre-emption accrued in the present case on the 14th November, 1960, the date of the Kabala under pre-emption, when Section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was not brought into operation but section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act was in force. In the circumstances the learned Advocate for the petitioner has submitted that the application for pre-emption should be deemed to be an application under, section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act, although the same has been purported to have been filed under section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

 6. Sattar, J, (as he then was) sitting singly in the case of Huzzat Ali Vs. Imamuddin Bepari 13 D.L.R. (Dhaka) page 819 held that an application for pre-emption filed after Chapter V of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act had come into operation must be governed by the rule of limitation prescribed by Section 96 of the said Act. This view of the warned Judge has been over ruled by a Division Bench of Dacca High Court in the case of Abdul Malek Vs. Abdur Rahman 19 D.L.R. (Dacca) page 318 in which the following view was expressed :— 

 "We are of the view that a right of pre-emption accrued before the repeal of the Bengal Tenancy Act does not cease to be a right under the repealed Act by virtue of section 8 of the Bengal General Clauses Act, 1899 and that the said right can in no manner be affected by the new act, since in terms of the Act of 1899 the new Act is to be considered as if it has not been passed. An applicant seeking to enforce his right of pre-emption accrued under section 26F of the old Act, is, therefore, entitled to the rule of three years limitation as was available to him before the repeal". 

 Although the application was described as under section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, I do not think that such a mis-description of the provision of law or misquotation of a particular section of an Act will stand in the way of the said application being considered to be under the relevant law which is applicable to the case in question. I am, therefore of the view that the learned Advocate for the petitioner is correct in con-tending that this application for pre-emption should regarded as an application under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act and the provisions of the said Act should be applied for the purpose of determining the question of limitation raised in the case. 

 7. Mr. Akram Hossain Amin, the learned Advocate for the petitioner next contends that the application being under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act and the co-sharer applicant having claimed that he was a non-notified co-sharer the period of limitation in such a case is not 4 months from the date of the knowledge as prescribed under section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, but three years from the date of sale as has been laid down by a Special Bench of the Calcutta High Court in the case of Asmat Ali Sharif Vs. Mujahar Ali Sardar and another 52 Calcutta weekly Notes page 64. It has been held in the said case that the case of non-notified cosharers having not been provided in the Bengal Tenancy Act nor there having been any specific provision in regard to such a case in the Limitation Act, the residuary provision of Article 182 of the Schedule to the Limitation Act shall apply. The learned Advocate for the petitioner contends that the starting point of limitation being the date of sale which was the 14th November, 1960 the period of limitation has come to an end on the expiry of three years from the said date and the present application having been filed after more than four years 7 months is hopelessly barred by limitation. 

 8. Mr. B. N. Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite parties has not seriously disputed the applicability of the provisions of the Bengal Tenancy Act to the present application for pre-emption, but he has contended that the period of limitation as prescribed under Article 182 of the Schedule of the Limitation Act shall be extended in the present case as the applicant had been suffering from a disability as contemplated in section 6 of the Limitation Act during the entire period from the date of accrual of the cause of action till the filling of the application. 

 9. The contention of the learned Advocate has raised a question of limitation of some nicety. The period of limitation prescribed under the Bengal Tenancy Act is of only 4 months from the date of service of the notice and it was a special or local law within the meaning of section 29 of the Limitation Act. Section 29(2) embodies the following provisions: 

 11. The said provision has application only in the case where any special or local law prescribes for any suit appeal or application a period of limitation different from the period prescribed therefor by the First Schedule in the limitation Act. The Bengal Tenancy Act does not provide for any period of limitation in respect of any application made by a non-notified co-sharer. According to the Special Bench decision of Calcutta High Court in Asmat Ali's case the period of limitation shall be three years, as prescribed under Article 182 of the First Schedule of the Limitation Act. The present case is that of a non-notified co-sharer. It is therefore, clear that it cannot be said that the Bengal Tenancy Act prescribes in respect of this particular application a period of limitation different from the period prescribed therefor by the Limitation Act. 

 19. Mr. Akram Hossain Amin, the learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that the original vendor purported to sell the land as a including the share of his brother and therefore he sound not be allowed to claim the right of pre-emption as a co-sharer. On a perusal of the document, however, I find that although he purported to sell the entire land, it was made clear in the deed that the property belonged to two brothers and the purchaser purchased the property with his eyes open.  We are not concerned here with any case as to whether, in view of the recitals in the Kabala, the opposite party No. 1 was not entitled succeed to the property of his deceased brother. This question cannot be decided in a summary proceeding like this under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act 1, therefore, do not find any substance in this contention of the learned Advocate.
